  ➜  the-dev-squad git:(cli-changes) ✗  cat src/lib/modelAdapters/index.ts
  import ClaudeCliAdapter from './claudeCliAdapter';
  import OpenAIHttpAdapter from './openaiHttpAdapter';
  import OpenClaudeCodeAdapter from './openClaudeCodeAdapter';
  import OpenClaudeAdapter from './openClaudeAdapter';
  import LMStudioAdapter from './lmStudioAdapter';
  import ClaudeCodeRouterAdapter from './claudeCodeRouterAdapter';
  import OllamaAdapter from './ollamaAdapter';
  import OpenWebUIAdapter from './openWebUIAdapter';
  import OpenAICompatAdapter from './openAICompatAdapter';
  import type { ModelAdapter } from './ModelAdapter';
  
  /**
   * Simple adapter factory for the pipeline runner.
   *
   * Recognizes a small set of well-known provider identifiers and returns a
   * corresponding ModelAdapter instance. Returns null when no matching adapter
   * is known.
   */
  export function getModelAdapter(provider?: string): ModelAdapter | null {
    const p = (provider || 'claude-cli').toLowerCase();
  
    if (p === 'claude-cli' || p === 'claude') {
      return new ClaudeCliAdapter();
    }
  
    if (p === 'occ' || p === 'open-claude-code' || p ===
  '@ruvnet/open-claude-code') {
      return new OpenClaudeCodeAdapter();
    }
  
    if (p === 'openclaude' || p === '@gitlawb/openclaude') {
      return new OpenClaudeAdapter();
    }
  
    if (p === 'openai-http' || p === 'openai') {
      return new OpenAIHttpAdapter();
    }
  
    if (p === 'lm-studio' || p === 'lmstudio') {
      return new LMStudioAdapter();
    }
  
    if (p === 'ccr' || p === 'claude-code-router') {
      return new ClaudeCodeRouterAdapter();
    }
  
    if (p === 'ollama') {
      return new OllamaAdapter();
    }
  
    if (p === 'openwebui' || p === 'open-webui') {
      return new OpenWebUIAdapter();
    }
  
    if (p === 'openai-compat' || p === 'openai-compatible') {
      return new OpenAICompatAdapter();
    }
  
    // Unknown provider
    return null;
  }
  
  export default getModelAdapter;

  Most important root causes I found
  
  1. Hydration error
  Cause:
  - `selectedProvider` was being derived from client-only state early enough to
  change the first client render.
  - timestamps/local time formatting also created server/client differences.
  
  Fix:
  - defer provider restoration until after mount
  - make timestamp rendering hydration-safe until the client is mounted
  
  Files:
  - page.tsx
  - page.tsx
  
  2. “Refresh goes back to Claude Code CLI”
  Cause:
  - there were two bugs:
    - provider restore happened after provider list loading in a way that could
  fall back to the first available provider
    - model persistence wrote the old model into the newly selected provider’s
  storage key before the new provider’s model list finished loading
  
  Fix:
  - provider restore now happens safely after mount
  - selected model is only persisted if it is valid for the current provider’s
  active `modelOptions`
  
  Files:
  - page.tsx
  - page.tsx
  
  3. LM Studio showing 25 models while you saw 8 in logs
  Cause:
  - those were two different LM Studio endpoints:
    - configured app endpoint: `http://10.2.0.90:1234` → 25 models
    - localhost endpoint: `http://localhost:1234` → 8 models
  
  This was not one server disagreeing with itself; it was the app talking to the
  saved remote host while you were looking at localhost.
  
  Fix:
  - UI now shows the resolved endpoint directly beside the model count
  
  Files:
  - route.ts
  - page.tsx
  - page.tsx
  
  4. Manual LM Studio worked but pipeline LM Studio failed
  Cause:
  - orchestrated runs spawn from `~/Builds/<project>`, so the shim path was
  being resolved relative to the project dir instead of the repo root.
  
  Fix:
  - all HTTP-backed adapters now resolve the shim from the workspace/repo path
  
  Affected adapters:
  - lmStudioAdapter.ts
  - ollamaAdapter.ts
  - openWebUIAdapter.ts
  - openAICompatAdapter.ts
  - openaiHttpAdapter.ts
  - claudeCodeRouterAdapter.ts
  - helper in ModelAdapter.ts
  
  5. Chat box greying out after a failed response
  Cause:
  - failed send paths weren’t always clearing the per-agent “sending” lock.
  
  Fix:
  - wrapped send paths with proper try/catch/finally and surfaced `chatError`
  
  Files:
  - page.tsx
  - page.tsx
  
  6. Why LM Studio pipeline still doesn’t behave like Claude Code CLI
  This is the big one.
  
  The infrastructure problems are mostly fixed now. The remaining failures are
  model/runtime behavior issues.
  
  What the LM Studio smoke runs now prove:
  - Agent A starts
  - it reads files
  - it uses tools
  - it persists a session
  - it stays in the orchestrator correctly
  - it no longer bypasses Bash restrictions
  - but this specific local model still:
    - emits malformed tool names sometimes (`[TOOL_CALLS]Read`,
  `TOOL_CALLS_Grep`)
    - tries disallowed commands
    - can hang long enough to hit the HTTP timeout
    - on some resumed sessions, LM Studio/model prompt templates may reject the
  raw message history shape
  
  So the current blocker is not “provider selection is not wired.”
  It is “this local model/provider combination is not yet as reliable at long,
  multi-turn, tool-using pipeline execution as Claude CLI.”
  
  Why Claude CLI feels different
  - Claude Code already has:
    - stable tool-call semantics
    - stable resume/session behavior
    - built-in hook enforcement
    - better compliance with long multi-step orchestration prompts
  - local small-ish models may answer single chats fine, but break down under:
    - many tool calls
    - resume turns
    - longer context
    - strict role discipline
    - exact tool naming
  
  Direct answers to your architecture questions
  
  Where variables are set
  Client:
  - provider/model selection state:
    - page.tsx
    - page.tsx
  - storage keys centralized in:
    - providerStorage.ts
  
  Main keys:
  - provider: `devsquad.selectedProvider`
  - pipeline model per provider: `devsquad.selectedModel.<provider>`
  - per-agent override: `devsquad.selectedModel.<provider>.<agent>`
  
  Client → API:
  - use-pipeline.ts
    - `sendChat(...)` sends `model` + `modelProvider`
    - `startPipeline(...)` sends `model`, `modelProvider`, `agentModels`
  
  Server persistence:
  - route.ts
    - pipeline-mode chat persists incoming provider/model into state
  - route.ts
    - persists provider/model/per-agent overrides before starting run
  - pipeline-control.ts
    - writes pipeline-events.json
  
  Pipeline state:
  - pipeline-events.json
    - `selectedProvider`
    - `selectedModel`
    - `agentModels`
    - `sessions`
    - `events`
  
  Execution:
  - orchestrator.ts
    - chooses `state.agentModels?.[agent] || state.selectedModel`
    - chooses `state.selectedProvider`
  - runner.ts
    - maps provider → adapter
    - spawns child process
  - index.ts
    - adapter factory
  
  How the 5 agents actually run
  It does not open 5 visible Claude windows.
  
  What it really does:
  - the orchestrator runs phased workflow
  - each agent turn is a spawned child process
  - sessions are tracked by ID in `pipeline-events.json.sessions`
  - for providers that support resume, later turns reuse the saved session ID
  - communication is not direct agent-to-agent socket chat
  - communication is mediated through:
    - shared workspace files
    - shared pipeline-events.json
    - orchestrator prompts/handoffs
    - per-agent session history
  
  So:
  - not 5 visible windows
  - not one single window reused for everything
  - it is process orchestration with per-agent sessions
  
  How memory works
  There are several memory layers:
  
  1. Runtime pipeline memory
  - pipeline-events.json
  - shared state for current run
  - statuses, phases, events, active agent, selected provider/model, sessions
  
  2. Per-agent conversation memory for HTTP-backed local providers
  - `~/.dev-squad-sessions/<sessionId>.json`
  - managed by http-runner-shim.mjs
  - used for `--resume`
  
  3. Workspace/file memory
  - `plan.md`
  - `checklist.md`
  - code files
  - test files
  - project artifacts
  
  4. devSquadMemory
  - this is not the main runtime engine
  - it is repo knowledge / RAG / notes / analysis / diagnostics
  - useful for docs and research, but not the core live pipeline state machine
  
  Why you “can message each agent manually” but the automatic pipeline still
  fails
  Manual mode is much easier:
  - one prompt
  - one response
  - maybe a few tool calls
  - human chooses next step
  
  Pipeline mode is much harder:
  - multi-turn
  - role discipline
  - resume support
  - strict sequencing
  - reliable tool-use over long context
  - phase transitions A→B→C→D→E
  
  So manual success does not imply full pipeline success.
  
  Provider-by-provider reality
  
  LM Studio
  How it’s used:
  - discovery:
    - `GET /api/v1/models`
    - fallback `GET /v1/models`
  - execution:
    - `POST /v1/chat/completions`
  - adapter:
    - lmStudioAdapter.ts
  - execution path:
    - through http-runner-shim.mjs
  
  Current state:
  - wired correctly
  - endpoint visible in UI
  - manual works better
  - pipeline starts and tools run
  - remaining issue is model/template reliability for long agentic runs
  
  Ollama
  How it’s used:
  - discovery:
    - `ollama list`
    - `/api/tags`
    - `/v1/models`
  - execution:
    - `/v1/chat/completions`
  - adapter:
    - ollamaAdapter.ts
  - also uses HTTP shim
  
  Why it may fail:
  - daemon not reachable
  - model not suitable for tool-heavy multi-turn use
  - local models may not honor tool format consistently
  
  Claude Code Router (CCR)
  How it’s used:
  - adapter:
    - claudeCodeRouterAdapter.ts
  - normal Anthropic models can go through `ccr code`
  - non-Anthropic/local models now bypass into the HTTP shim using the mapped
  provider endpoint from `~/.claude-code-router/config.json`
  
  Why it was failing:
  - bad trailing-arg parsing
  - local model names rejected by Claude-side validation before request routing
  - missing or ambiguous provider mapping in CCR config
  
  What changed:
  - prompt/arg parsing fixed
  - local-model HTTP-shim bypass added
  
  OpenClaude
  How it’s used:
  - adapter:
    - openClaudeAdapter.ts
  - spawns `openclaude` or `npx @gitlawb/openclaude`
  - discovery is mostly config/env driven because the CLI is not a great
  machine-readable model lister
  
  Why it may not work how you expect:
  - it is a wrapper CLI, not automatically an LM Studio/Ollama bridge
  - if you expect local model routing, that must exist in its own config/routing
  path
  
  OCC / open-claude-code
  How it’s used:
  - adapter:
    - openClaudeCodeAdapter.ts
  - spawns `occ` or `npx @ruvnet/open-claude-code`
  - discovery is inferred from banner/env/known model defaults
  
  Why it may not work:
  - it is primarily a wrapper path, often Bedrock-oriented
  - not a generic “local provider” by itself unless configured that way
  externally
  
  Why sometimes “functions” or tools are not seen
  Several reasons:
  1. model capability
  - some local models do not reliably emit valid tool calls
  
  2. malformed tool names
  - fixed partly with normalization
  
  3. provider prompt-template incompatibility
  - LM Studio/model template can reject certain history shapes on resume
  
  4. missing hook parity
  - Claude CLI had stronger enforced guardrails
  - I patched the biggest gap today: local-provider Bash guardrails
  - full 1:1 parity with every write/edit/web restriction from approval-gate.sh
  is not yet mirrored inside the shim
  
  5. long context / resume instability
  - local models may degrade over many tool turns
  
  Hardcoded models vs discovery
  Current behavior now:
  - discovery-first
  - fallback second
  
  Route:
  - route.ts
  
  For LM Studio/Ollama/OpenWebUI:
  - discovery is preferred
  - fallback lists are intentionally empty/near-empty so stale hardcoded lists
  don’t mislead you
  
  For CLI wrappers like `claude-cli`, `ccr`, `occ`, `openclaude`:
  - fallback model names still exist because reliable machine-readable discovery
  is weak or unavailable
  
  Why this was necessary:
  - some CLIs do not expose a clean `list models` command
  - showing nothing would make the UI unusable
  - but for LM Studio/Ollama, live discovery is the better path and that’s what
  the app now prefers
  
  Per-agent models
  Yes, this is supported now.
  
  UI:
  - main page per-agent selects: `data-testid="agent-model-A"` etc
  - squad page per-agent overrides also present
  
  Flow:
  - UI stores per-agent override in localStorage
  - use-pipeline.ts sends `agentModels`
  - `start-pipeline` persists it
  - orchestrator uses per-agent override first, pipeline-wide model second
  
  Verified:
  - Playwright now confirms `/api/start-pipeline` receives:
    - provider
    - selected model
    - per-agent overrides

  - Agent A starts planning
  - reads files
  - uses Glob/Grep/Read
  - no longer silently gets away with Bash
  - Bash attempts from A are blocked
  - run no longer fails immediately from shim path issues
  - remaining failures are model/runtime quality issues:
    - malformed tool names
    - timeouts
    - occasional LM Studio prompt-template incompatibilities on resume

  That means the core plumbing is now much healthier than before.
  The remaining problem is not “the app isn’t sending to LM Studio.”
  It is “this LM Studio model/runtime is not yet robust enough for full

  About the repeated `grep: empty (sub)expression`
  That is not an app bug.
  It came from this shell regex:
  - `grep -n "^\|"`
  
  On your system that’s an invalid expression.
  
  Use one of these instead:
  - `grep -n '^' file`
  - `nl -ba file`
  - `sed -n '=' file`

  ## Files to Create
  
  ### 1. `src/orchestrator.ts`
  **Purpose**: Core orchestration logic for model loading and task execution.
  
  ```typescript
  // src/orchestrator.ts
  import { initializeModel } from "huggingface-transformers"; // Replace with
  actual dependency
  import { TaskRunner } from "@langchain/core"; // Example alternative
  
  type OrchestrationConfig = {
      modelId: string;
      taskRunnerConfig?: Record<string, any>;
  };
  
  class LmStudioOrchestrator {
      private model: any;
      private taskRunner: TaskRunner;
  
      constructor(config: OrchestrationConfig) {
          this.taskRunner = new TaskRunner(config.taskRunnerConfig || {});
      }
  
      async initializeModel(modelId: string): Promise<void> {
          try {
              this.model = await initializeModel(modelId);
              console.log(`Model initialized: ${modelId}`);
          } catch (err) {
              throw new Error(`Failed to initialize model: ${err.message}`);
          }
      }
  
      public async executeTask(taskName: string, inputs?: any): Promise<any> {
          try {
              const result = await this.taskRunner.runTask(taskName, inputs);
              console.log("Task executed successfully:", taskName);
              return result;
          } catch (err) {
              throw new Error(`Task execution failed: ${err.message}`);
          }
      }
  }
  
  // Example usage
  (async () => {
      const config = { modelId: "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2" }; //
  Replace with real model ID
      const orchestrator = new LmStudioOrchestrator(config);
  
      await orchestrator.initializeModel(config.modelId);
      const result = await orchestrator.executeTask("generate_embeddings", {
  text: "Test sentence." });
      console.log(result);
  })();
  ```
  
  ---
  
  ### 2. `src/utils/Logger.ts`
  **Purpose**: Utility class for logging orchestration events.
  
  ```typescript
  // src/utils/Logger.ts
  export class Logger {
      constructor(private name: string) {}
  
      info(message: string): void {
          console.log(`[${this.name}] INFO: ${message}`);
      }
  
      error(message: string, err?: Error): void {
          const errorMsg = err ? err.message : message;
          console.error(`[${this.name}] ERROR: ${errorMsg}`);
      }
  }
  ```

  ---
  
  ### Research Summary
  
  The concept of an **orchestrator smoke run** for **LM Studio** involves
  leveraging LM Studio's **headless core (`llmster`)** to create a lightweight,
  server-based agent framework capable of running local LLMs in isolation. Key
  findings:
  
  #### 1. **Core Components**
     - **LM Studio Headless Mode (`llmster`)**
       - A headless runtime for LM Studio designed for servers, CI/CD pipelines,
  and remote environments.
       - Supports Linux, macOS, Windows (WSL), and cloud VMs.
       - Provides API access via `serve` mode for local model orchestration.
  
     - **Smoke Testing**
       - Typically involves validating basic functionality: starting the
  runtime, querying models, and ensuring no crashes or errors.
       - Often includes checks for:
         - Model loading.
         - API endpoint availability.
         - Basic prompt-response cycles.
  
  #### 2. **Key Implementation References**
     - **LM Studio Docs**: Headless mode is explicitly documented as a core
  feature for server deployments ([docs](https://lmstudio.ai/docs/headless)).
     - **GitHub Repositories**:
       -
  [`itspriyanshuks17/llmster_lsmstudio`](https://github.com/itspriyanshuks17/llmster_lsmstudio):
  Provides installation and usage guidance for `llmster`.
       - **Smoke Testing Frameworks**: While not directly tied to LM Studio, the
  concept of smoke testing in CI/CD pipelines (e.g., running a minimal agent
  workflow) is widely applicable.
  
  #### 3. **Unresolved Gaps**
     - No direct source code or repository for an **LM Studio-specific
  orchestrator** was found.
     - The workspace (`~/Builds/orchestrator-smoke-run-lm-studio`) does not
  contain any existing files related to LM Studio's agent framework, `llmster`,
  or smoke testing logic.
  
  #### 4. **Next Steps**
     To proceed with planning:
     - Confirm if the goal is to build a **custom orchestrator** for LM Studio
  (e.g., using `llmster` + a lightweight agent layer) or to integrate an
  existing framework.
     - Clarify whether the smoke run should focus on:
       - Validating `llmster`'s basic functionality (e.g., model loading, API
  endpoints).
       - Implementing a minimal agent workflow (e.g., chaining prompts across
  models).
  
  ---
  ### Next Action
  Please confirm:
  1. **What is the exact purpose of the orchestrator?** Is it to:
     - Validate `llmster` for server deployments?
     - Build a lightweight agent framework for LM Studio?
     - Integrate with an existing tool (e.g., `smolagents`)?
  2. **Should the smoke run focus on:**
     - Basic model loading and API checks?
     - A minimal workflow (e.g., prompt → response → validation)?
  
  This will help refine the plan to align with LM Studio's architecture and
  requirements.

  - Symptom/evidence: mis-parsed tool blocks, many normalization helpers in

  - Root cause: regex/heuristic parsing duplicated across shim/orchestrator/UI;
  function-calling fields not prioritized.
  - Impact: unknown/misspelled tools, failed tool invocations, agent loops or
  silent failures.
  - Fix (P0): central canonical tool registry `src/lib/toolRegistry.ts`
  (aliases, canonical names, safety metadata) + two-stage parser: (1) provider
  function-calling fields, (2) strict JSON code-block extraction, (3) strict
  fallback regex. Replace `parseToolCallsFromText`, `normalizeToolName` uses in
  http-runner-shim.mjs, orchestrator.ts, route.ts.
  - Tests: unit tests for many noisy variants + integration cases in
  test-http-runner.mjs.
  - Estimate: 1–2 days.
  
  2) Sessions trimmed naively → lost tool results on resume
  - Symptom/evidence: resumed sessions missing tool outputs; sessions live at
  `~/.dev-squad-sessions/*.json`; summary notes naive char-count trimming in
  `trimSessionContext`.
  - Root cause: trimming based only on character budget drops high-value
  assistant/tool-result messages.
  - Impact: agents lose context and re-run tools or fail tasks;
  non-deterministic behavior after resume.
  - Fix (P0): implement importance-scoring trimmer in http-runner-shim.mjs:
    - Always preserve system prompts, last N assistant/user messages, and all
  tool results.

  heuristic) instead of deleting.

  result snapshot, timestamp).
  - Tests: resume + multi-turn stability tests, deterministic resume harness.
  - Estimate: 2–3 days.
  
  3) Provider-config staleness / caching issue
  - Symptom/evidence: recent change removed caching for immediacy; risk of extra
  I/O or previous stale cache behavior; file is provider-config.json and code
  providerConfig.ts.
  - Root cause: no safe invalidation strategy.
  - Impact: stale UI/provider list or excessive disk reads.

  optional `fs.watch` debounce; expose force-reload API.
  - Tests: unit test that edits provider-config.json and confirms reload.
  - Estimate: 0.5 day.
  
  4) Agents try shell commands but pipeline blocks them (BASH blocked)

  Concrete design and code pointers (high-level pseudo / small snippets)
  - Tool registry interface (TypeScript sketch for `src/lib/toolRegistry.ts`):
  ```ts
  export type ToolDef = {
    id: string;                // canonical: "WebFetch"
    aliases: string[];         // ["webfetch","web-fetch","web_fetch"]
    requiresApproval: boolean;
    egressRisk: "none"|"low"|"high";
    handler: string;           // shim handler name
  };
  
  export const TOOL_REGISTRY: Record<string,ToolDef> = {
    WebFetch: { id: "WebFetch", aliases: ["webfetch","web-fetch"],
  requiresApproval: true, egressRisk: "high", handler: "webfetch" },
    // extend...
  };
  
  export function normalizeToolName(raw: string): string | null {
    const key = raw.trim().toLowerCase();
    for (const def of Object.values(TOOL_REGISTRY)) {
      if (def.id.toLowerCase() === key) return def.id;
      if (def.aliases.includes(key)) return def.id;
    }
    return null;
  }
  ```
  
  - Provider-config safe caching (sketch for providerConfig.ts):
  ```ts
  let _cached: { mtimeMs: number; data: any } | null = null;
  export async function readProviderConfigs(path = "provider-config.json") {
    const stat = await fs.promises.stat(path);
    if (_cached && _cached.mtimeMs === stat.mtimeMs) return _cached.data;
    const raw = await fs.promises.readFile(path, "utf8");
    const data = JSON.parse(raw);
    _cached = { mtimeMs: stat.mtimeMs, data };
    return data;
  }
  fs.watch("provider-config.json", { persistent: false }, () => { _cached =
  null; });
  ```

  You're right that the orchestration layer matters a lot — but you're only half
  right. The software (tools, agent loop, prompting strategy, error recovery,
  tool definitions, and supervision) is crucial, but the model itself is the
  single biggest factor in how well an agentic system actually performs on
  complex, long-running tasks.
  
  Here's the breakdown:
  
  Model vs. Orchestration
  Orchestration decides what the agent tries to do: which tools it has, how it
  loops, how it recovers from failure, how a supervisor delegates to
  specialists, how context is managed.
  The model decides whether it can do it well: reasoning quality, following
  complex instructions over 50+ turns, avoiding dumb loops, making good tool
  choices, writing correct code on the first or second try, maintaining
  coherence in a large codebase.
  Claude Code looks so strong because both are excellent: Anthropic tuned Claude
  heavily for tool use and long-horizon reasoning, plus they built a very solid
  agent loop around it. When you swap in a weaker local model (even with the
  exact same tools and orchestration), the whole system gets dumber fast — bad
  research choices, hallucinated URLs, weak plans, unnecessary bash attempts,
  failing to apply its own edits correctly. That's what you're seeing.
  
  Your Repo Specifically (the-dev-squad)
  From the logs you shared, this appears to be a local-first multi-agent web UI
  with:
  
  A main page + squad page
  Pipeline mode (orchestrated multi-agent runs) vs manual mode
  Support for LM Studio / Ollama / local providers via an http-runner-shim.mjs

  Per-agent model selection (recently improved in manual mode)
  Tools like file ops, bash, web search/fetch (the recent patches added web
  parity for local providers)
  Provider config system, state management in use-pipeline.ts, and UI locking
  logic that was causing the greyed-out issues
  The architecture is trying to give you a Claude-Code-like squad experience
  (supervisor + specialists) but running against local models through LM Studio.
  The recent fixes you applied — removing config cache, adding timeouts, fixing
  sticky UI locks, adding web tools to the shim, and exposing per-agent
  selectors in manual mode — were exactly the right plumbing changes.
  
  Why It Still Feels Weaker Than Real Claude Code
  Even with perfect plumbing:
  
  Smaller local models (Mistral, Ministral, etc.) have weaker chain-of-thought
  and tool-calling reliability over long sessions.
  Context handling and instruction following degrade faster.
  They need much stronger, more explicit prompting and guardrails than Claude
  does.
  Tool use quality is lower — they pick worse actions and recover from mistakes
  more poorly.
  The orchestration can only amplify what the underlying model is capable of.
  Good scaffolding on a weak model still loses to good scaffolding on a strong
  model.
  
  Practical Advice for Offline/Local Setup

  Got it. I’ve reviewed your version of the repo⁠GitHub. Here’s a clear,
  no-fluff explanation of how the backend actually works and how the agents
  communicate.
  
  Core Concept
  This system gives Claude a supervised dev team (S=Supervisor, A=Planner,
  B=Reviewer, C=Coder, D=Tester, optional E=Security Auditor). All agents work
  in the same project folder (~/Builds/<project>).
  
  The key idea is the plan is the contract. Agent A writes a very detailed
  plan.md, Agent B tears it apart until it’s perfect, then the plan gets locked.
  After that, Coder C must implement exactly what’s in the plan — no deviating.
  
  How Agents Communicate With Each Other
  Agents do not talk in normal text to each other. They only communicate using
  structured JSON signals.
  
  Examples of these signals:
  
  { "status": "approved" }
  { "status": "questions", "questions": }
  { "status": "issues", "issues": [...] }
  The orchestrator (pipeline/orchestrator.ts) is the middleman. It works like
  this:
  
  It launches each agent as a separate Claude Code CLI process with its own role
  file (role-a.md, role-b.md, etc.).
  Each agent is told (through its system prompt) to output JSON when it wants to
  communicate with another agent or end its turn.
  The orchestrator reads the output, parses the JSON, and decides what to do:
  If it sees status: "approved", it advances to the next phase.
  If it sees status: "questions", it sends those questions back to the previous
  agent.
  If it sees status: "issues", it sends them to the agent that needs to fix
  them.
  This creates controlled loops (A ↔ B until the plan is locked, C ↔ D until
  tests pass).
  
  What Makes This Happen
  Three things work together to make the agents communicate this way:
  
  Role definition files (role-a.md, role-b.md, etc.) — These are very strict
  system prompts that tell each agent exactly what their job is and that they
  must output structured JSON when handing off.
  The orchestrator — This is plain TypeScript code (not an LLM). It runs the
  loop, parses JSON, routes messages, and controls phase progression. It’s
  deterministic.
  The PreToolUse hook (.claude/hooks/approval-gate.sh) — This runs before every
  tool call. It checks which agent is calling the tool (PIPELINE_AGENT
  environment variable) and blocks anything that agent isn’t allowed to do. This
  enforces the rules.
  Backend Summary (Your Current Version)
  Frontend: Next.js app with two views (Office View and Squad View)
  State: Managed in src/lib/use-pipeline.ts
  API layer: Next.js API routes handle starting/stopping and chat
  Execution: The real work happens in pipeline/orchestrator.ts + Claude Code CLI
  Local support: Your version added http-runner-shim.mjs to let LM Studio/Ollama
  work instead of just Claude Code. The shim translates between what the
  orchestrator expects and what local models output.
  Bottom line: The intelligence still comes from the model, but the structure
  (strict roles + JSON-only handoffs + locked plan + hook enforcement) is what
  makes the squad behave in a disciplined way instead of just being six separate
  chats.

  Here's exactly how this system works.
  
  The Orchestrator Is Completely Outside the Claude Terminals
  Yes — the orchestrator is a separate TypeScript program
  (pipeline/orchestrator.ts). It is not running inside any Claude Code terminal.
  
  It works like this:
  
  The orchestrator launches six separate Claude Code processes (one for each
  agent: S, A, B, C, D, E).
  Each process runs in its own isolated environment with its own .claude folder
  containing that agent's specific role-*.md file.
  The orchestrator talks to each process through standard input and output
  (stdin/stdout), exactly like any other command-line tool.
  It reads the output from each Claude process line by line, looks for JSON, and
  decides what to do next. This is how it "understands" five (or six) different
  Claude terminals at once — it's the parent process watching all of them.
  
  How Communication Actually Happens
  There is no direct connection between the Claude terminals. They cannot see or
  talk to each other.
  
  Communication only happens through the orchestrator:
  
  Claude A outputs some JSON (for example: {"status": "questions", "questions":
  [...]}).
  The orchestrator reads that JSON from A's stdout.
  The orchestrator then feeds a message into Claude B's stdin, telling B what A
  said.
  Claude B thinks, outputs its own JSON, and the orchestrator routes it back to
  A if needed.
  This creates a controlled ping-pong between agents, all managed by the
  orchestrator.
  
  How It Bypasses Claude Code's Single-Terminal Limitation
  Normal Claude Code CLI is designed for one human ↔ one Claude conversation in
  one terminal.
  
  This repo bypasses that by:
  
  Running multiple independent Claude processes at the same time.
  Using the orchestrator as a "conductor" that controls the conversation flow.
  Forcing each Claude to output structured JSON signals instead of normal chat
  (this is heavily trained into the role files).
  Using the approval-gate.sh hook (in .claude/hooks/) to enforce strict rules on
  what each agent is allowed to do. This hook reads the PIPELINE_AGENT
  environment variable to know which agent is making a tool call.
  How Your Version Uses This Architecture
  Your version keeps the exact same orchestrator from the original. The core
  communication system hasn't changed.
  
  What you added/changed:
  
  The UI (Next.js frontend) to control everything.
  Support for local models (LM Studio, Ollama, etc.) through
  http-runner-shim.mjs. Instead of spawning real Claude Code processes, the shim
  pretends to be Claude Code — it accepts the same prompts, runs them against
  your local model, and translates the local model's output back into the JSON
  format the orchestrator expects.
  Fixes to make the UI more reliable (timeouts, better state management,
  per-agent model selectors in manual mode).
  So in your version:
  
  When using Claude Code → uses the original multi-process method.
  When using LM Studio → the orchestrator talks to your shim instead of real
  Claude, and the shim talks to LM Studio.
  The fundamental difference is that Claude was heavily trained to follow these
  strict JSON handoff rules. Local models are much worse at consistently
  outputting clean JSON and staying in character, which is why the system feels
  weaker even though the architecture is the same.

  Here's the clear truth about what's happening.
  
  How the Original Claude Code Version Works
  The system relies on two layers:
  
  The Orchestrator (pipeline/orchestrator.ts) — This is a regular TypeScript
  program running completely outside the Claude terminals. It spawns multiple
  Claude Code CLI processes and talks to them through stdin/stdout.
  The Role Files (role-*.md) — These are very long, strict system prompts given
  to each agent. They tell the agent:
  Exactly what their job is
  When to hand off work
  Exactly what JSON to output when they want to communicate (e.g. {"status":
  "approved"}, {"status": "questions", "questions": [...]})
  The orchestrator constantly reads the output of each Claude process. When it
  sees clean JSON with a status field, it parses it and decides what to do next
  (activate next agent, send questions back, move to next phase, etc.).
  
  This works well with Claude because Claude is extremely good at following
  these complex instructions and outputting clean JSON consistently.
  
  Your Shim + Offline Models Problem
  Your shim (http-runner-shim.mjs) is trying to pretend to be a Claude Code CLI
  process. The orchestrator talks to the shim, the shim talks to LM Studio, and
  it tries to translate the responses back into the JSON signals the
  orchestrator expects.
  
  This is where it breaks:
  
  The offline models are much worse at consistently outputting the exact JSON
  format the orchestrator is looking for.
  Even though the models support tool calling, they frequently:
  Output messy JSON (extra text, wrong structure, missing fields)
  Forget to output the status field
  Mix normal text with JSON
  Fail to follow the strict handoff rules in the role files
  When the orchestrator doesn't see a clean status: "approved" or status:
  "questions" signal, it doesn't know to move to the next agent. So the pipeline
  gets stuck even though individual agents are responding.
  
  Why Pipeline Mode Fails But Individual Chats Work
  Individual manual chats work because you're directly talking to one model. But
  pipeline mode requires strict, consistent, structured handoffs between agents.
  Local models are currently too unreliable at this disciplined behavior.
  
  What You Can Do
  Here are the realistic options:
  
  Improve the shim — Make it more aggressive at extracting and cleaning JSON
  from the model's messy output. Add fallback parsing that looks for JSON blocks
  even when the model adds extra text.
  Strengthen the role prompts for local models — Create separate, simpler role
  files for offline models that are less strict and give more examples of
  correct JSON output.
  Add a dedicated "JSON cleaner" step — This is similar to your idea of a 7th
  agent. The shim could take the model's raw output and force it into clean JSON

  Stay in Manual mode — This is currently the most reliable way to use local

  model and the strict orchestrator.

  "Here's the clear truth about what's happening.
  How the Original Claude Code Version Works
  The system relies on two layers:
  
  The Orchestrator (pipeline/orchestrator.ts) — This is a regular TypeScript
  program running completely outside the Claude terminals. It spawns multiple
  Claude Code CLI processes and talks to them through stdin/stdout.
  The Role Files (role-*.md) — These are very long, strict system prompts given
  to each agent. They tell the agent:
  Exactly what their job is
  When to hand off work
  Exactly what JSON to output when they want to communicate (e.g. {"status":
  "approved"}, {"status": "questions", "questions": [...]})
  
  The orchestrator constantly reads the output of each Claude process. When it
  sees clean JSON with a status field, it parses it and decides what to do next
  (activate next agent, send questions back, move to next phase, etc.).
  This works well with Claude because Claude is extremely good at following
  these complex instructions and outputting clean JSON consistently.
  Your Shim + Offline Models Problem
  Your shim (http-runner-shim.mjs) is trying to pretend to be a Claude Code CLI
  process. The orchestrator talks to the shim, the shim talks to LM Studio, and
  it tries to translate the responses back into the JSON signals the
  orchestrator expects.
  This is where it breaks:
  
  The offline models are much worse at consistently outputting the exact JSON
  format the orchestrator is looking for.
  Even though the models support tool calling, they frequently:
  Output messy JSON (extra text, wrong structure, missing fields)
  Forget to output the status field
  Mix normal text with JSON
  Fail to follow the strict handoff rules in the role files
  
  When the orchestrator doesn't see a clean status: "approved" or status:
  "questions" signal, it doesn't know to move to the next agent. So the pipeline
  gets stuck even though individual agents are responding.
  Why Pipeline Mode Fails But Individual Chats Work
  Individual manual chats work because you're directly talking to one model. But
  pipeline mode requires strict, consistent, structured handoffs between agents.
  Local models are currently too unreliable at this disciplined behavior.
  What You Can Do
  Here are the realistic options:
  
  Improve the shim — Make it more aggressive at extracting and cleaning JSON
  from the model's messy output. Add fallback parsing that looks for JSON blocks
  even when the model adds extra text.
  Strengthen the role prompts for local models — Create separate, simpler role
  files for offline models that are less strict and give more examples of
  correct JSON output.
  Add a dedicated "JSON cleaner" step — This is similar to your idea of a 7th
  agent. The shim could take the model's raw output and force it into clean JSON
  before giving it to the orchestrator.
  Stay in Manual mode — This is currently the most reliable way to use local
  models with this system.
  
  Your recent 64 changes mostly improved the UI, timeouts, and manual mode
  support. The core pipeline + local model reliability issue is still
  fundamentally about the model's ability to follow these strict structured
  output rules consistently.
  Would you like me to focus on one specific improvement — like how to make the
  shim better at cleaning JSON, or how to modify the role files for local
  models?Interruptedlet's focus on all four. I want to focus on all four and

  for all four options to make your offline/local models work much more reliably
  with the pipeline.
  
  Improve the Shim (Best short-term fix)
  Goal: Make http-runner-shim.mjs smarter at cleaning up messy output from local
  models before giving it to the orchestrator.
  Concrete Plan:
  Add a JSON extraction layer after receiving the model's response. Use regex to
  find the first {...} block, then try to parse it.
  If parsing fails, implement a fallback parser (strip markdown, remove
  explanatory text, fix common errors like trailing commas).
  Add retry logic: if the output doesn't contain a valid status field, send a
  follow-up message to the model like "You must respond with valid JSON
  containing a 'status' field. Try again."
  Add logging so you can see exactly what raw output the model is producing vs.
  what the shim sends to the orchestrator.
  Make the shim accept a role parameter and prepend stronger JSON instructions
  specific to local models.
  
  This is the highest leverage change because it sits directly between the weak
  model and the strict orchestrator.
  2. Strengthen Role Prompts for Local Models
  Goal: Create a separate set of role files optimized for weaker models.
  Concrete Plan:
  
  Duplicate the current role files (role-a-local.md, role-b-local.md, etc.).
  Make them much more explicit:
  Add many more few-shot examples of correct JSON handoffs.
  Add strong instructions like "You MUST end every response with a JSON object
  containing exactly a 'status' field. Do not add any text after the JSON."
  Lower the complexity of the role (shorter plans, simpler handoff rules).
  
  Modify the orchestrator (or shim) to load the -local.md version when using LM
  Studio/Ollama.
  Add temperature=0 and top_p=0.1 settings for local runs to reduce randomness.
  
  Local models need much more hand-holding than Claude.
  3. Add a Dedicated JSON Cleaner Layer (Your 7th Agent Idea)
  Goal: Insert a deterministic "translator" between the model and the
  orchestrator.
  Two ways to implement this:
  Option A (Recommended): Enhance the shim to act as the cleaner.
  
  After the model responds, the shim doesn't just forward the text — it analyzes
  it and forces it into one of the expected formats (approved, questions,
  issues, etc.).
  
  Option B: Add a real 7th process.
  
  Create a small local Python/Node script that takes raw model output and uses a
  strong local model (or even simple regex + rules) to convert it to clean JSON.
  The orchestrator would talk to this cleaner process instead of directly to the
  weak model.
  
  This is essentially "put a smart wrapper around the dumb model."
  4. Stay in Manual Mode + Hybrid Approach (Most reliable today)
  Goal: Accept current limitations and build a usable workflow.
  Concrete Plan:
  
  Keep pipeline mode for Claude only.
  For local models, stay in Manual mode with per-agent model selectors (you
  already improved this).
  Add a "Quick Handoff" button in the UI that manually sends the proper JSON
  signal to the next agent.
  Use your strongest local coding model only for specific roles (e.g., Coder),
  while keeping Supervisor as Claude when possible.
  Build a "Local Pipeline Lite" that only uses 2–3 agents instead of the full
  squad.
  
  Overall Recommendation & Next Steps
  The best path right now is to combine Option 1 (better shim) + Option 2
  (local-specific role files). These two changes directly attack the root cause:
  local models producing inconsistent structured output that the orchestrator
  can't understand.
  The reason the pipeline doesn't advance automatically is almost certainly that
  the orchestrator is waiting for a clean {"status": "approved"} (or similar)
  that it never receives from your local models.

  My Honest Recommendation
  Don't add a 7th agent. That adds latency and another point of failure.

  and the orchestration layer. Call it the JSON Coercion / Repair Layer.

  It’s fast and reliable (no extra LLM call).
  It aggressively fixes bad output (unclosed brackets, missing fields, trailing
  commas, wrong keys).
  If it can’t fix it cleanly, it sends a very targeted retry message back to the
  original agent telling it exactly what’s wrong ("You returned invalid JSON.
  The schema requires a 'tool_calls' array. Fix it.").
  This is much more effective than hoping a weak local model gets it right on
  its own.
  Layer Architecture I Suggest
  Provider Layer — LM Studio (or any OpenAI compatible endpoint)
  HTTP Shim — your existing http-runner-shim.mjs (only handles raw HTTP + basic
  normalization)
  New JSON Repair Layer — deterministic code that validates against your tool
  schemas and repairs output
  Orchestration Layer — stays mostly as-is, but now receives much cleaner
  structured data
  This new middle layer becomes the single place where all communication between
  agents gets cleaned up and standardized.

  Use LM Studio’s built-in structured outputs (they support response_format with
  json_schema exactly like OpenAI). This pushes the constraint down to the model
  level — often the cleanest solution.

  Research Summary (What Actually Exists)
  The most battle-tested solution for turning messy LLM output (text,
  pseudo-JSON, XML-style, markdown, trailing commas, missing brackets, etc.)
  into clean structured JSON is jsonrepair by josdejong.
  
  It's written in TypeScript, has excellent TypeScript types, works perfectly in
  Node.js, and is specifically good at handling LLM garbage.
  It fixes a huge list of common issues: missing quotes, trailing commas, single
  quotes, smart quotes, comments, markdown fences, Python True/False/None,
  truncated JSON, and more.
  Other popular ones like json_repair (Python) and llmjson (Rust) exist, but
  jsonrepair is the clear winner for your TypeScript codebase.
  The consensus from Reddit and GitHub is clear: use a fast deterministic repair
  library first, then fall back to a targeted retry prompt only when the repair
  fails. Adding another full agent or LLM in the middle is overkill.

  My Honest Take
  jsonrepair by josdejong is still one of the strongest and most practical
  options for a TypeScript project like yours. It's actively maintained (recent
  updates in 2026), has 2.3k+ stars, and is specifically tuned for LLM garbage.
  The most interesting newer approach is agentjson — it goes beyond simple
  repair by trying to understand the intent of the output. However, since it
  doesn't have a native JavaScript version, we'd have to call it through a
  bridge, which adds complexity.
  The real best practice in 2026 is moving toward constrained generation
  (telling the model exactly what schema to follow at generation time) instead
  of repairing after the fact.
  Simple Recommendation for Your Project
  For now, the simplest and most effective thing is to use josdejong's
  jsonrepair as the core of your new layer. It's reliable, has no extra
  dependencies, and works exactly where you need it (inside

  Progress update — quick summary of what I did and next choices.
  
  What I did
  - Audited the repo for the JSON-repair / tool-registry surface (confirmed both
  a runtime scripts/* implementation and a TypeScript port under src/lib).
    - Key files found: scripts/json-repair.mjs, src/lib/jsonRepair.ts,
  scripts/tool-registry.mjs, src/lib/tool-registry.json,
  scripts/http-runner-shim.mjs.
  - Implemented a pragmatic, non-invasive improvement: when tool-argument
  parsing fails, the shim now emits a clear tool_result error and pushes a
  focused, single-shot repair prompt back to the model (one retry only). File
  changed:
    - http-runner-shim.mjs — added argRepairRetries, a retry prompt, and a small
  control flow to let the model repair malformed JSON arguments.
  - Ran the repo tests locally:
    - node test-jsonrepair.mjs — passed
    - npx tsx test-tool-registry.mjs — passed
    - npx tsx test-http-runner.mjs — passed
  - Created a tracked todo list for the consolidation work (stored via the repo
  todo tool).
  
  Why this change
  - It gives models a deterministic, targeted opportunity to fix malformed JSON
  arguments rather than silently failing; minimal token cost and low complexity.
  
  Current blockers / observations
  - Duplicate implementations exist (runtime scripts vs TS port). The shim
  currently imports the runtime scripts/json-repair.mjs, not jsonRepair.ts —
  risk of divergence.
  - Consolidation requires picking one of two practical approaches (see options
  below). CI currently relies on npx tsx — CI must make tsx available if we
  require TypeScript imports at runtime.
  - check-duplicate-tools.py reports duplicate tool names from local Copilot
  debug snapshots (this is local workspaceStorage noise, not repo manifests).
  
  Options / recommended next steps (pick one)
  - Option A (recommended, canonical): Consolidate to src/lib as the single
  source of truth.
    - Add a small build step (tsc or esbuild) to produce a runtime JS artifact
  (dist/jsonRepair.cjs).
    - Make json-repair.mjs a thin wrapper that imports the compiled artifact.
    - Benefits: single-authoritative TS source, less drift long-term.
    - Work: add build script + small wrapper + update README + CI build step.
  - Option B (fast, low risk): Keep runtime scripts as-is and enforce parity.
    - Add unit parity tests that compare json-repair.mjs and jsonRepair.ts
  outputs on a set of regression examples.
    - Add CI job that runs parity tests and the existing smoke tests (npx tsx
  ...).
    - Benefits: minimal runtime changes, fast to ship.
  - Option C (future enhancement): Add a tiny deterministic validator that
  validates repaired JSON against tool schemas and, when deterministic repair
  fails repeatedly for a tool, optionally call a very small specialist LLM
  repairer (only as fallback).
  
  If you want me to proceed now
  - I can implement Option A (canonical build + wrapper) or Option B (parity
  tests + CI). Tell me which and I will:
    - For Option A: add a build script, create wrapper, update shim to import
  compiled artifact, and run tests.
    - For Option B: add parity tests + GH workflow job to run tests and fail on
  divergence.

  What I found
  - The repo already has provider plumbing for Claude CLI, CCR, OpenClaude, occ,
  Ollama, LM Studio, Open WebUI, OpenAI-compatible, and `openai-http`.
  - There is **no OpenCode adapter yet**.
  - `projectDir` / cwd scoping is already threaded through the pipeline in
  several places, but there is no dedicated “locked working directory”
  abstraction.
  - The supervisor flow exists, but the language and handoff logic still need
  tuning so it feels like a supervisor/autonomous team run, not just a planner.
  - There is no queue/draft-message UI yet for typing while a provider is still
  responding.
  - LM Studio and Ollama already have support for model discovery and
  OpenAI-compatible execution; Open WebUI is also already partially supported.
  
  Plan I saved for implementation
  1. Create a fresh branch from `master` and baseline the current behavior.
  2. Add a first-class OpenCode adapter and wire it into provider discovery,
  model lists, and the UI.
  3. Harden the JSON/structured-output layer so local providers normalize into
  the repo’s tool-call format instead of leaking freeform text.
  4. Make working-directory scoping explicit and enforced through pipeline
  state, runner cwd, and provider context.
  5. Restore/expand squad and office model controls, including per-agent
  dropdowns and host/port/api-key fields for HTTP-style providers.
  6. Tune the supervisor handoff so “start planning” really drives the full
  autonomous pipeline.
  7. Do a real manual LM Studio validation against `10.2.0.90:1234`:
     - message the supervisor
     - ask for a tic-tac-toe build
     - issue “start planning”
     - watch the run proceed end-to-end
  8. Update devSquadMemory with what worked, what failed, and the recommended
  architecture for the provider middle layer.
  9. Add only targeted tests for the changed surface, not a full broad E2E sweep
  unless needed.
  
  Key decisions captured
  - Use cwd / `projectDir` as the hard boundary, with prompt/context
  reinforcement as backup.
  - Treat OpenCode as a new provider adapter, starting from whatever
  command/runtime is actually available locally.
  - Prefer native structured-output support when providers offer it; otherwise
  normalize through repair logic.

  already has per-agent model selection state management wired end-to-end, with
  localStorage persistence scoped per-provider — it just lacks UI components to
  render the dropdowns.
  
  The agentic pipeline's core blocker in cli-changes ("agentic still is not
  working") traces directly to the adapter pattern's ChildProcess interface
  mismatch. json-provider-layer sidesteps this entirely by having the runner
  spawn the shim directly. The shim itself is solid — ~600 lines implementing a
  multi-turn agentic loop with tool execution, per-agent permission guards,
  context trimming, and JSON repair — but needs hardening for production use
  with small models.
  
  Branch Architecture Comparison
  Dimension	main	cli-changes	json-provider-layer
  Provider dispatch	Claude CLI only	Adapter factory → 9 class files
  (STUBS)	3-way if/else in runner.ts
  Model discovery	None	Per-adapter discoverModels()	Centralized listModels() in
  catalog

  Per-agent models	Orchestrator reads agentModels	Same orchestrator

  The 12 Decision-Point Debates
  1. Provider Abstraction: Adapter Classes vs. Catalog + Direct Dispatch
  cli-changes created ModelAdapter interface with spawn() → ChildProcess,
  factory in index.ts, and 9 adapter files (claude, lm-studio, ollama,
  openai-http, openai-compat, openclaude, openclaude-code, claude-code-router,
  open-webui).
  
  Agent	Position
  FOR adapters	OOP extensibility — adding a provider = adding a class. Each
  adapter encapsulates discovery, spawn, availability. Standard pattern.
  AGAINST adapters	Fundamental type mismatch: spawn() returns ChildProcess but
  LM Studio/Ollama/OpenAI are HTTP APIs, not CLI processes. All 8 non-Claude
  adapters are explicitly STUBS (README says so). LM Studio adapter's spawn()
  just shells out to http-runner-shim.mjs — making it a pointless wrapper around
  the thing that does the actual work. 9 files for zero additional
  functionality. isAvailable() returns true unconditionally on LM Studio —
  defeats purpose.
  FOR catalog	json-provider-layer's provider-catalog.ts is pure typed data (275
  lines). listModels() handles ALL providers. Runner has 3 clear paths. 2 files
  replace 9.
  AGAINST catalog	Adding a provider touches runner dispatch (but it's a trivial
  if/else, not a class hierarchy).
  
  🏆 VERDICT: json-provider-layer wins decisively. The adapter pattern is a
  category error for HTTP APIs.
  
  2. The HTTP Runner Shim (http-runner-shim.mjs)
  Both branches share this ~600-line file. This is the real Claude CLI
  replacement.
  
  Agent	Position
  FOR	Brilliant translation layer — accepts Claude CLI args, emits Claude Code
  stream-json events. Orchestrator needs ZERO changes. Implements real tools
  (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep, WebSearch, WebFetch). Per-agent
  permission guards replicate approval-gate.sh for any provider. Agentic loop
  with MAX_AGENT_TURNS=30. Context trimming. JSON repair. Session persistence.
  AGAINST	~600 lines of raw JavaScript — no type safety. Dual responsibility
  (arg translation + agentic loop). Text-based tool call extraction is fragile.
  Single-shot fallback for non-function-calling models kills agent capability.
  No streaming during execution. No exponential backoff. No token counting —
  relies on error responses to detect overflow.
  
  🏆 VERDICT: Right approach, needs hardening. Convert to TypeScript. Add
  per-agent turn limits, streaming, token counting, backoff.
  
  3. Per-Agent Model Selection
  Layer	Status
  Orchestrator (main + both branches)	✅ `const activeModel =
  state.agentModels?.[agent] \	\	state.selectedModel \	\	DEFAULT_MODEL`
  State persistence (json-provider-layer)	✅
  writeAgentModelOverride(selectedProvider, agent, value) in localStorage
  React hook (json-provider-layer)	✅ use-provider-runtime.ts exposes agentModels
  + setAgentModel(agent, value)
  UI components	❌ Nothing renders dropdowns per agent
  Model validation	❌ No check that selected agent model is actually available
  Fallback on unavailability	❌ Not implemented
  
  🏆 VERDICT: 80% done. Backend plumbing is solid. Missing: UI dropdowns,
  availability validation, graceful fallback.
  
  4. Provider Configuration & URL Resolution
  json-provider-layer's providerConfig.ts implements a clean priority chain:
  
  Code
  
  Copy
  env vars → provider-config.json (mtime-cached + fs.watch) → CCR auto-detection
  → DEFAULTS
  Agent	Position
  FOR	Handles real-world deployment: env overrides for CI/CD, file config for
  local, CCR integration auto-discovers LM Studio from Claude Code Router. File
  watching for live updates. 174 lines, clean separation.
  AGAINST	fs.watch() unreliable on some platforms (wrapped in try/catch). CCR
  auto-detection is LM Studio-specific. DEFAULTS hardcode localhost.
  
  🏆 VERDICT: Production-ready. Minor: make DEFAULTS configurable.
  
  5. Model Discovery
  Agent	Position
  FOR centralized (json-provider-layer)	listModels() handles ALL providers.
  Tries OpenAI format (/v1/models → {data:[{id}]}) AND Ollama format (/api/tags
  → {models:[{name}]}). Self-loop protection. 3s/5s timeouts.
  AGAINST	Uses curl via child process (not Node-native). No caching. Claude
  models hardcoded to Opus 4.1 + Sonnet 4.5.
  
  🏆 VERDICT: Correct approach. Add TTL-based caching, consider native fetch.
  
  6. Small Model Detection & Lite Roles
  isSmallModel() in orchestrator checks name patterns: nano, mini, tiny, small,
  size patterns like "1b"–"4b".
  
  Agent	Position
  FOR	Auto-detects when models need shorter prompts. ROLE_LITE mapping →
  role-a-lite.md etc. resolveRoleFile() picks lite vs full transparently.
  Critical for your 1B/4B LM Studio models.
  AGAINST	Name-based detection is brittle — custom model names won't match. No
  runtime capability testing. No UI indication that lite mode activated. Lite
  role files may not exist on disk.
  
  🏆 VERDICT: Essential for your setup, fragile implementation. Add model
  metadata-based detection (check /v1/models response for parameter count if
  available), add UI badge.
  
  7–12. Quick Verdicts
  Decision	Winner	Key Reason
  Tool permission system	Shim's JS guards	Only viable path for non-Claude
  providers; make configurable via JSON
  Agentic loop design	Shim's multi-turn loop	Functional but needs per-agent turn
  limits, streaming, backoff
  JSON repair	Keep, convert to TS	Essential for small models; add test coverage
  UI state management	use-provider-runtime.ts	Complete hook, needs loading/error
  states
  State persistence	Split: localStorage (UI) + pipeline-events.json
  (pipeline)	Already implemented this way in json-provider-layer
  Docker vs Host	HostRunner for HTTP providers	Correct — Docker can't reach
  local LM Studio without host networking
  
  Recommended Architecture for New Branch
  Base: feature/json-provider-layer — cherry-pick from cli-changes only what's
  needed.

  Priority Implementation Order
  UI: Agent model dropdowns — The hook is ready, just needs React components

  still exists

  failures

  Critical Watch Items for Small Models (1B/4B)
  Your 1B and 4B LM Studio models will hit specific issues:
  
  Function calling: Most 1B models don't support OpenAI tool/function calling
  API. The shim falls back to single-shot mode → agents lose tool use
  capability. Mitigation: Use the 4B model for agents that need tools (A, C, D)
  and 1B for review-only agents (B, E).
  
  JSON signal extraction: Small models produce malformed JSON signals. The
  json-repair.mjs handles some cases but extractSignal() in the orchestrator may
  still fail. Mitigation: Add retry with explicit "respond ONLY with JSON"
  re-prompt.
  
  Context window: 1B models typically have 2K–4K context. Role files + plan
  content may exceed this immediately. Mitigation: isSmallModel() → ROLE_LITE is
  the right fix, but verify lite role files exist on disk. Create them if not.
  
  Auto-unload after 1 min: LM Studio's auto-unload means the model may not be
  loaded when the next agent needs it. The shim will get a connection refused or
  loading delay. Mitigation: Add retry with exponential backoff in the shim's
  API call function.
